title: Some Power Games That Happen in Schools
author: Debbie Thompson
summary: Debbie Thompson draws on 24 years in English secondary schools to analyze how senior leaders who were once excellent teachers can slip into power-game dynamics that undermine and exhaust the teachers in their charge. She traces the mechanism: leadership roles bring invisible pressures (Ofsted, governors, budget), create identity shifts from practitioner to controller, and surround leaders with deference that insulates them from honest feedback. Insecure leaders—those who are unsure of their authority—are most prone to the gotcha observation, the moving goalposts, and the inconsistent standards that Thompson identifies as the most damaging patterns, because unpredictability is more exhausting than high expectations. The piece is a compassionate but unflinching account of how institutional structures transform capable people and why the costs fall disproportionately on experienced classroom teachers.
points: Senior leaders who were once excellent teachers are not immune to power dynamics; institutional pressures and identity shifts make teacher-undermining behavior structurally predictable.
The leadership bubble—where people defer, ideas go unchallenged, and the leader's perspective becomes self-confirming truth—is a normal consequence of positional power, not personal malice.

Insecure leaders are most prone to power games: the gotcha observation, shifting expectations, and unpredictable standards are symptoms of leaders who manage through fear because they fear losing control.
Unpredictability is the specific mechanism that wears teachers down—high expectations can be met, but standards that shift without warning make professional competence impossible to demonstrate.

The system loses good teachers as a consequence: the process of being managed out typically causes mental health damage, and the institution retains the leader while losing experienced classroom practitioners.
quotes: From my own experience, I know that power can turn people in education into self-centred individuals.

They are no longer judged by their teaching, but by their control of the teachers who work for them and their control of the school. They are rewarded for their decisiveness even if the decision they made wasn't based on consulting teachers who were affected by it.

Power tends to change the social environment around senior leaders. People laugh at their jokes more. They stop being challenged, and often their ideas are accepted too quickly. Over time, this can create a bubble where they believe their perspective is the objective truth.
Those leaders who aren't sure about leading can often slip into power games because they are scared of what could happen if they don't step in and manage and control how staff work.

Teachers can cope with high expectations, they cope with them every day. What wears them down is the sense that the rules are not stable, and that their professional worth is being assessed through a lens they cannot control.
